samples.summary: New web OAuth `state` cookie is not host-locked (`__Host-` prefix / explicit `path`+`secure`), so a sibling subdomain can fix it and defeat the new CSRF binding
samples.evidence: `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE_NAME = 'wafflebase_oauth_state'` (cookies.ts:16) is set at github-auth.guard.ts:77 with only `{httpOnly, secure: NODE_ENV==='production', sameSite:'lax', maxAge}` — no `__Host-` prefix, no explicit `Path=/`, and `Secure` conditional on NODE_ENV. The entire new web-flow binding is `timingSafeEqualString(cookie, stateToken)` in auth.controller.ts:261. Cookies are not origin-scoped: anything that can write a cookie for the registrable domain (XSS or takeover on any `*.wafflebase.io` host, or a plaintext sibling host when `Secure` is off) can set `Domain=.wafflebase.io; wafflebase_oauth_state=<attacker value>`. The attacker then knows the state value, mints a GitHub `code` against their own account, and navigates the victim to `/auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code>&state=<attacker value>`; the cookie comparison succeeds and the victim is seated in the attacker's account — precisely the login-CSRF/session-fixation this change exists to stop. `__Host-` (which forces Secure, host-only, Path=/) is the standard mitigation and the repo's own design notes say the sibling CLI-state work uses it. Note `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` also means the state cookie travels in cleartext in any deployment where NODE_ENV is not exactly `production`.

samples.summary: The `?mode=cli` OAuth entry point still has no browser-side binding: a hostile page can start a CLI OAuth round trip in the victim's browser with an attacker-chosen loopback port
samples.evidence: `canActivate` returns early with a cookie-mirrored state only when `mode !== 'cli'` (github-auth.guard.ts:67-83). The CLI branch (lines 85-103) mints a server-side state for any unauthenticated request and sets no cookie, so `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker port>&nonce=<attacker nonce>` is fully CSRF-able. A page in the victim's browser can trigger that navigation; GitHub silently re-authorizes (previously granted app), the callback mints a single-use CLI code for the *victim's* account (auth.controller.ts:148) and 302s the victim's browser to `http://127.0.0.1:<attacker-chosen port>/callback?code=...`, i.e. an authorization code for the victim's account delivered to a port the attacker names on the victim's machine — a code-leak primitive for anything the attacker can get to listen (or log) on that loopback port, with no consent step and no user-visible artifact. Same endpoint also lets any unauthenticated caller grow `CliAuthStore.states` (5-minute TTL, only the 120/min global throttler bounds it). The in-tree justification for not fixing this here (docs/tasks/active/20260803-cli-system-exit-code-lessons.md, 'PR #786 already ships that binding — a `wafflebase_cli_state` cookie, a framing-proof consent interstitial, PKCE, `__Host-` prefixes') is not verifiable on this branch: grepping the working tree for `cli_state`, `__Host-`, `interstitial` and `consent` finds none of it, so as shipped here the CLI OAuth entry is unbound.

samples.summary: `rawRequest` quotes the raw transport error message without the `redactDetail` scrubbing every other CLI network error gets, so a presigned image URL or `--server` userinfo can be echoed to stderr/CI logs
samples.evidence: `fetchOrThrow` (packages/cli/src/errors.ts) deliberately runs the underlying error text through `redactDetail(detail, url)` because 'undici and Node echo the request URL verbatim for some failures'. The new `rawRequest` fallback in image-fetcher.ts:615-623 builds the same class of message with `redactUrl(target)` for the URL but interpolates `cause.message` unredacted. Image `src` values are attacker-influenced and routinely carry presigned signatures in the query string; an undici error that echoes the full request URL therefore puts the signature (and any `user:pass@` from `--server`) straight onto stderr, defeating the redaction the rest of the change adds.

samples.summary: The `--allow-unbound-callback` security downgrade is published in the agent-facing schema registry, contradicting the design's own rule that it be discoverable only where an attacker has no say
samples.evidence: `docs/design/cli.md` and the login-timeout comment (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:460-477) argue at length that the downgrade flag must be discoverable only via `--help` and the README, 'never as advice triggered by an unauthenticated request', because taking that advice completes a login fixation. registry.ts:48 nonetheless exports the flag in the machine-readable command schema that AI agents consume — the same agents that also read attacker-influenced document content and error output. An agent that is talked into `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback` reproduces exactly the outcome the invariant timeout message was written to prevent.

samples.summary: Residual SSRF: when an egress proxy is configured, the gate's approved addresses are discarded and the proxy re-resolves the attacker-chosen hostname, so DNS rebinding still reaches the proxy's network
samples.evidence: `hopDispatcher` (image-fetcher.ts:494-515) returns a `ProxyAgent` and drops `pinnedAgent` whenever `http_proxy`/`https_proxy`/`all_proxy` applies. `assertFetchableImageUrl` resolves the name once; the proxy resolves it again at connect time. A ~0s-TTL nameserver under the document author's control answers the gate with a public address and the proxy with an internal one, and the proxy fetches it — the gate's verdict is not enforced on that path. The trade-off is documented in the source and in docs/design/cli.md and a one-line stderr notice is emitted per run, so this is disclosed rather than hidden; recording it because a proxied `docs export` of an attacker-supplied document is still an SSRF probe against the proxy's reachable network, and the notice is easy to miss in CI.

samples.summary: `isPrivateAddress` misses the IPv4-translated `::ffff:0:0/96` spelling and the 6to4 relay anycast range, and `isInternalHostname` is not applied to trailing-dot FQDNs
samples.evidence: `isPrivateAddress` (image-fetcher.ts:161-206) folds `::ffff:x:y` and `::x:y` (words[0..4] all zero) into the IPv4 rules, but `::ffff:0:7f00:1` — the RFC 2765 IPv4-translated form — has words[4] = 0xffff, so `words.slice(0,5).every(w=>w===0)` is false and it falls through every branch to `return false`. Similarly `192.88.99.0/24` (6to4 relay anycast) is not in `isPrivateIPv4`. Separately, `isInternalHostname` (line 82) compares `hostname` without stripping a root dot, so `metadata.google.internal.` and `localhost.` skip the name check (they are still caught by the resolved-address check, so this one is defence-in-depth only). Each is a narrow spelling gap in a control whose whole job is 'the same address in every spelling'; exploitability depends on the host's routing for these prefixes, hence low confidence.

The attacker then knows the state value, mints a GitHub `code` against their own account, and navigates the victim to `/auth/github/callback?code=<attacker code>&state=<attacker value>`; the cookie comparison succeeds and the victim is seated in the attacker's account — precisely the login-CSRF/session-fixation this change exists to stop. `__Host-` (which forces Secure, host-only, Path=/) is the standard mitigation and the repo's own design notes say the sibling CLI-state work uses it. verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. cookies.ts:16 defines the state cookie name without a `__Host-` prefix, and baseCookieOptions() (cookies.ts:29-35) supplies only {httpOnly, secure: NODE_ENV==='production', sameSite:'lax'} — no host-locking. github-auth.guard.ts:75-81 sets the web OAuth state with those options plus maxAge, and auth.controller.ts:255-266 makes that unsigned cookie the sole binding for the callback (cookieParser is registered with no secret at main.ts:64, so the cookie is not signed either). Because cookies are not origin-scoped, an attacker controlling any sibling host on the registrable domain (or any plaintext sibling when NODE_ENV != 'production', where Secure is off) can set a Domain-scoped `wafflebase_oauth_state` of known value and then navigate the victim to the callback with a code minted against the attacker's GitHub account; SameSite=Lax permits the top-level GET (intentionally, per cookies.ts:24-27), the timing-safe compare passes, and the victim is seated in the attacker's account — the exact login-CSRF/session-fixation this control exists to stop. I searched for any compensating guard (domain option, signed cookies, session binding, host checks) across packages/backend/src and found none; docs/design/rest-api.md:383 documents the mitigation as only httpOnly+SameSite=Lax, confirming host-locking was not implemented. The finding's only inaccuracy is cosmetic: Express defaults Path=/ so the missing explicit `path` is immaterial; the missing `__Host-` prefix is the real weakness. Squarely in the auth/CSRF lane and a clear security weakness in a newly added security control, so blocking at major.

verdict.reason: Verified in-tree: GitHubAuthGuard binds only the web flow to the browser (github-auth.guard.ts:67-83 sets OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE_NAME). The `?mode=cli` branch (github-auth.guard.ts:85-103) accepts any unauthenticated request, validates only port range and nonce format, mints a server-side CliAuthStore state and sets no cookie — so a cross-site top-level navigation to /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker>&nonce=<attacker> is fully CSRF-able. The callback then explicitly skips the web state check for CLI states (auth.controller.ts:126-128), mints a single-use code for the victim's account (auth.controller.ts:148) and 302s the victim's browser to http://127.0.0.1:<attacker-chosen port>/callback?code=... (auth.controller.ts:155-157). Searched wide for the claimed existing binding and found no counterexample: repo-wide grep for cli_state/__Host-/interstitial/consent yields only docs and a dictionary file; cookies.ts:16-35 documents that only one OAuth state cookie exists and that CLI deliberately has none; main.ts:30-79 installs no CSRF/origin/Sec-Fetch middleware (CORS does not constrain top-level navigations); frontend login-form.tsx:27 links plain /auth/github with no CLI interstitial; github.strategy.ts:59-66 merely forwards req.__oauthState. The CLI-side nonce check (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:246) does not help because the attacker picks both port and nonce. This is an auth/CSRF weakness within the security lane, major impact (code-leak primitive plus unauthenticated growth of CliAuthStore.states).

mergedFrom.summary: The web OAuth state cookie uses one fixed name with no per-flow scoping, so any cross-site-initiated `/auth/github` navigation overwrites an in-flight login's state

finding.summary: CLI-mode OAuth entry (`?mode=cli`) still has no browser-side CSRF binding, while the same guard now adds one for the web branch — a cross-site-initiated navigation can make a victim's browser emit a valid Wafflebase auth code to an attacker-chosen loopback port
finding.evidence: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` splits at `if (mode !== 'cli')` (github-auth.guard.ts:67). The web branch mints a random state AND mirrors it into `wafflebase_oauth_state` so the callback can prove the browser started the login (github-auth.guard.ts:75-81, verified at auth.controller.ts:250-267). The CLI branch (github-auth.guard.ts:85-101) mints only a server-side state entry and sets no cookie, and `githubAuthCallback` skips `consumeWebOAuthState` entirely whenever `cliState?.mode === 'cli'` (auth.controller.ts:126-128). `GET /auth/github` is unauthenticated and reachable by top-level navigation. Attack: a hostile page navigates the victim to `https://api.example/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker-picked 1024-65535>&nonce=<attacker nonce>`; GitHub silently re-approves the already-authorized app; the callback mints a CLI code for the VICTIM's account and 302s the victim's browser to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<victim code>&nonce=<attacker nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:143-157). The 60s single-use code is now in the victim's browser history and in the request log/URL of whatever local service listens on that port. The nonce added by this change does not defend here because the attacker supplies it. The port range check (1024-65535) is the only limit on the target. This is pre-existing behaviour that the change relocated/renamed rather than introduced, but the change is precisely the one that adds a browser binding to the sibling branch and leaves this one without.

verdict.reason: Every claimed location checks out. GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate branches at github-auth.guard.ts:67; the web branch mints a random state AND mirrors it into the OAUTH_STATE cookie (75-81), while the CLI branch (85-101) creates only a server-side CliAuthStore entry with no browser-side binding whatsoever. auth.controller.ts:126-128 skips consumeWebOAuthState (the only browser binding, defined at 250-267) whenever cliState?.mode === 'cli', and 143-157 mints a 60s single-use code for the authenticated victim and 302s the victim's browser to http://127.0.0.1:<caller-supplied port>/callback?code=...&nonce=<caller-supplied nonce>. GET /auth/github (auth.controller.ts:96-110) is unauthenticated and reachable by cross-site top-level navigation, so a hostile page can force this whole round trip with no proof the browser started it; the port range check (github-auth.guard.ts:86) is the only constraint. The CLI-side nonce check (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:398-410, nonceMatches 320-325) does not guard this, because in the attack the attacker chooses both the port and the nonce, so no upstream/other call site makes the path unreachable. Impact is a login-CSRF/auth-code-exposure primitive: the victim's exchangeable code (redeemable at POST /auth/cli/exchange, auth.controller.ts:167-183) is emitted to a caller-chosen loopback listener and into browser history/local access logs. The attacker cannot read the code cross-origin, which caps it at major rather than critical, but that is severity, not a refutation. The guard's own comment (lines 22-45) acknowledges the asymmetry as deliberate; documented intent is not a refutation ground. In lane (auth/CSRF/access control), real, and not already guarded.

mergedFrom.summary: The DNS-rebinding pin protecting the new SSRF gate is silently dropped for every hop whenever an egress proxy env var is set, so the gate's verdict and the connect-time resolution diverge

finding.summary: SSRF address pin is silently dropped whenever an egress proxy applies, re-opening DNS rebinding through the proxy's own resolution
finding.evidence: `hopDispatcher()` returns a `ProxyAgent` and never a `pinnedAgent` when `proxyForUrl(target)` matches (image-fetcher.ts:397-409). The file comment and `docs/design/cli.md` both claim "Dropping the pin there costs nothing that was ever held ... under a proxy the CLI performs no connect-time resolution at all." That is only half true: the proxy resolves the name instead, and its answer is not the answer the gate approved. Vector: an attacker who can edit/share a document sets `src=http://rebind.attacker/x` behind a nameserver with ~0s TTL. `assertFetchableImageUrl` (line 316) resolves it to a public address and allows it; the request is then handed to the operator's `http_proxy`, which re-resolves `rebind.attacker` and gets `169.254.169.254` (or an internal host). The proxy fetches it and the bytes are embedded in the PDF/DOCX/PPTX the victim reads — exactly the SSRF this gate exists to stop, on precisely the machines (corporate, proxy-only egress) where internal targets are most valuable. The gate's own resolution is not authoritative for the proxied hop, so nothing else constrains it. Mitigation would be to pass the gate's approved address as the connect target (or refuse to proxy names whose gate-time and request-time identity cannot be tied), rather than asserting the risk is nil.

verdict.reason: The mechanical core is present and reachable: hopDispatcher (packages/cli/src/docs/image-fetcher.ts:494-515) returns a ProxyAgent whenever proxyForUrl(target) matches and only reaches pinnedAgent(addresses) on the non-proxied branch (line 514), so on any machine with http_proxy/https_proxy/all_proxy set the gate's approved-address pin is not applied. createImageFetcher (lines 709-724) gates each hop with assertFetchableImageUrl (line 710) but then hands the request to the proxy, which re-resolves the attacker-chosen hostname; a ~0s-TTL nameserver can answer the gate publicly and the proxy with an internal/metadata address, and the fetched bytes are embedded in the exported PDF/DOCX/PPTX. I found no other check constraining that proxied hop, so neither 'already-guarded' nor 'not-present' applies to the vulnerable behavior itself, and SSRF is in this lens's lane. Caveat on the reviewer's evidence, which I checked and found inaccurate: the quoted comment text ("Dropping the pin there costs nothing that was ever held", "no connect-time resolution at all", "asserting the risk is nil") does not exist anywhere in the repo (grep returns no matches); image-fetcher.ts:469-478 and docs/design/cli.md:944-968 both state the residual risk is real rather than nil, and line 503 plus reportPinDropped (lines 685-697) emit a once-per-run stderr warning naming exactly this rebinding risk, so it is neither silent nor asserted to be harmless. Confidence is low because the residual is an explicitly documented, operator-warned tradeoff whose proposed mitigation (pinning the connect target through CONNECT) is not offered by proxy protocols, which makes its blocking status debatable — but documentation is not a guard, so I keep the finding.
